_comment: Mutation testing: breaks the source on purpose and checks the tests notice. A mutant that
leaves the suite green is a bug the tests cannot see — unlike line coverage, this cannot be
satisfied by executing code without asserting on it.
Full explanation, glossary and diagrams: docs/tools/mutation-testing.md. This file carries
only the reasoning behind the settings below.
A narrower scope than today's measured 65.69% over everything and 72.22% over covered code,
from 3324 mutants across 100 files in 85 minutes at the concurrency below. Controllers, the
runtime wiring, the tracer, `module.ts` and `seeds.ts` have since come back INTO scope (see
SCOPE), so the next run measures more code than that: expect a LOWER total, since what
returns is largely code no unit test imports, and a `covered` figure that is comparable
because no-coverage mutants do not enter it. mutation-baseline.json holds the per-file
record and is the gate that matters — `break` is only the collapse detector.
`incremental` stores each mutant's verdict in `reports/stryker-incremental.json` and reuses
it on
the next run when BOTH the mutated code and the tests covering it are unchanged. Only what
actually moved is re-tested, which is what makes a run affordable outside the nightly.
It buys that speed WITHOUT giving up signal, which is the whole reason it is preferred to
`ignoreStatic`. Every mutant still has a verdict; the verdict is reused rather than skipped.
`ignoreStatic: true` would be far faster still — Stryker reports ~20% of mutants here as
static and estimates they take ~96% of the run — but it drops those mutants from the report
entirely, which is a permanent blind spot over schemas, route tables and module-scope
objects. Speed bought with coverage is the one trade this file will not make.
That file is COMMITTED — CI can only reuse what is in the repo, and an ignored incremental
file makes this a local-only optimisation that looks enabled. `.gitignore` therefore reads
`reports/*` plus a negation for this one file, because git does not descend into an excluded
DIRECTORY: with plain `reports/` the negation is silently dead. See the note there.
A cache can go stale — a refactor that moves code between files, or a badly resolved merge —
so the nightly passes `--force` to ignore the stored results and rebuild from scratch. Fast
feedback on demand, a trustworthy full measurement every night.
A run re-executes the suite once per mutant, so it lives in .github/workflows/mutation.yml,
nightly and on demand. The PR-time gate is `npm run test:mutation:check`, which compares the
last report against mutation-baseline.json in under a second and runs no mutants at all.
`mutate` covers logic: `app` (the Express wiring), `infrastructure` (adapters, the http
pipeline, persistence), `kernel` (registry, events, the auth port and its guard) and every
module's model, repository, service, routes and supporting files.
The bar for EXCLUDING something is high, and it is not 'the tests would not kill it'. An
unkilled mutant is a finding; a file missing from the report is a blind spot, because a file
absent from the report reads exactly like a file with no survivors. Nor is cost a reason: a
mutant in code no test imports is reported NO COVERAGE without running anything, so leaving
untested code in scope is nearly free and is how the report stays honest about the gap.
So the only things excluded here are ones where a mutant could not mean anything to anyone:
- `*.fragment.ts` files are text slices of a committed document, assembled by
`npm run contracts:bundle`. NOTHING imports one — the assembled bundle is what runs — so
a mutant in a fragment is unobservable by construction, not merely unkilled.
- Each module's `index.ts` is a barrel: its mutants ask whether a re-export changed, which
is a question about the module system rather than about this code.
- `src/modules/*/tests/**` is test code, not the code under test.
Everything else stays in, INCLUDING code this runner cannot reach. `src/app/**` measured
0.00% on 2026-08-12 — 126 mutants, every one NO COVERAGE, not one survivor — and that zero
is kept deliberately: it is the visible, standing statement that the Express wiring is
exercised by tests/integration and tests/contract (excluded from this RUNNER by
`testPathIgnorePatterns`) and by no unit test at all. Read it with the `covered` column,
which is unaffected by it. Hiding that layer behind an exclusion would trade a true number
that looks bad for a prettier one that says nothing.
- Each module's `index.ts` is a barrel and `module.ts` is declarative registration; their
mutants ask whether a re-export changed. `seeds.ts` builds the demo dataset and runs
only under `db:seed`.
- `*.fragment.ts` files are text slices of a committed document, assembled by
`npm run contracts:bundle`. Nothing imports one; the bundle they build is what runs.
`testPathIgnorePatterns` above is the other half of the controller decision, and it has two
homes to cover because contract tests do: `tests/contract/` AND each module's own
`src/modules/<name>/tests/contract/`. Those suites drive the real app over HTTP against a
live database; under Stryker they fail in the dry run before a single mutant is tested.
The patterns are REGEXES, not globs — `[^/]+` is the module segment.
`contract-bundles.test.ts` is excluded for a different reason, and it is about the SANDBOX
rather than about the test. That file asserts each committed document is byte-identical to
the fragments it is assembled from. Stryker copies the project to `.stryker-tmp/sandbox-*`
and prepends `// @ts-nocheck` to every file there (`disableTypeChecks`), so the fragments it
reads have extra lines the committed bundle does not — the assertion compares bytes and can
never hold. Turning `disableTypeChecks` off is the wrong trade: `ts-jest` runs with
diagnostics ON, so a type-breaking mutant would fail to COMPILE, count as killed, and
inflate the score with kills no assertion earned. Excluding the file costs no coverage
either way — it exercises committed files and `scripts/`, and neither is in `mutate`.
`ignorePatterns` must NOT list public/**: the sandbox is the only filesystem the tests see,
and tests/unit/db/seed-fixtures.test.ts asserts every seed fixture's imageUrl resolves to a
committed file under public/images/seed/. Without it Stryker refuses to start at all.
`high`/`low` colour the report and nothing else. `break` is the only one that fails a run,
and it belongs at the bottom of the observed band so it answers 'has something collapsed'
rather than 'did the number move'. The real gate is per-FILE, in mutation-baseline.json — a
global percentage lets a strong file carry a weak one. Raise `break` only when a score
SUSTAINS a higher band; never lower it to make a run pass.
Read `total` against `covered` before spending effort. Far apart means mutants with NO
COVERAGE — write tests that reach the code. Close together means tests run it without
asserting — sharpen what exists. The single percentage hides which.
The ceiling is MEMORY, not cores: each worker is a separate process carrying a full test
runner and its own in-memory mongod, and the machine is in use while a run happens. 8 on a
32-core / 30 GB box leaves headroom deliberately; at 12, free RAM fell to ~6 GB and load
average hit 14. Lower it on a smaller machine rather than raising it on a bigger one.
CI overrides this: mutation.yml passes --concurrency 3, because a standard GitHub runner is
4 vCPU / 16 GB. The safe number is a property of the machine, not of the project.
A run strands one ~200 MB mongo-mem-* directory in /tmp per killed worker (Stryker SIGKILLs
a jest worker per timed-out mutant, so MongoMemoryServer.stop() never runs).
tests/support/global-setup.ts prunes the directories whose mongod is provably gone, never a
concurrent instance's live one — read that file before changing the sweep.
